I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
I should have protected others and I failed
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' directly conflicts with 'Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts' within the same maladaptive strategies node. Excessive work engagement and avoidance of work/study are opposing coping patterns and, without any qualifier distinguishing contexts, are clinically contradictory.

vignette: The clatter of a dropped cooler and the sharp crack of a broken crate echoed through the waterfront market that day. Kiana had been hauling nets near the slips when the argument escalated, and one assailant sprinted past her, the heavy thud of his footsteps echoing off the concrete while another fled on a rattling bicycle, its chain grinding and tires screeching against the damp asphalt. In that moment, Kiana's mind locked onto the failure: she had stood still while a life was almost taken. Her certainty that she should have protected him and feared she would lose control completely colored every subsequent sound. Whenever the wind caught a bicycle chain or distant footsteps matched the rhythm of the attack, those triggers immediately summoned the memory of the event, though it arrived not as a clear picture but as a suffocating wave of emotion without an image. The guilt of the recall clung to her chest, and the sudden auditory triggers began to dictate her daily movements, pushing her to work excessively on the trawler, filling every hour with hauling lines so she would never have to sit in silence. Because the triggers reinforced her fear of her own rage, they directly deepened her negative appraisals, convincing her she was fundamentally unsafe. Within weeks, the threat in her physiology became impossible to ignore. Her body would react to danger before her mind had even processed whether she was safe, a physiological hijacking that left her breathless and disoriented. The memory of the event, now stripped of any visual anchor, directly triggered this physiological threat response. In turn, the escalating threat symptoms fed back into her negative appraisals, deepening her conviction that her body was the enemy and that she had failed to protect others. The negative appraisal that she could not control herself only intensified the threat response, making her heart race faster at the mere suggestion of a delay. Because she could not concentrate on reading charts or navigating lines, she began to dread the trawler's engine delays, assuming something bad was happening whenever a repair took longer than expected. The threat response ensured that the memory would force its way into her mind uncontrolled, bypassing her attempts to focus, while the hyperarousal made ordinary bicycle sounds near the dock feel like immediate triggers. The overwork quickly bled into every corner of her life, becoming a rigid shield against the intruding memories. She would spend long hours on her phone or playing games once on shore, a screen escape that deliberately blocked out any quiet moment where her thoughts might surface. Her avoidance of sex with her boyfriend followed the same logic; intimacy required stillness, and stillness invited the emotional intensity of the event. Because she kept herself constantly occupied, the maladaptive strategies paradoxically starved her nervous system of safety signals, ensuring that the threat system remained hyperactive. The more she overworked and screenscaped, the more her body continued to react before her mind could intervene, and the harder it became to focus on routine tasks. This exhaustion eventually made her avoidant tactics feel necessary rather than harmful, trapping her in a cycle where the strategies themselves became the source of renewed threat and negative self-judgment. When the uncontrolled access of the memory finally breached her focus, it forced her to reach immediately for overwork or screen escape, while her conviction that she had failed to protect others pushed her to avoid sex entirely. The relentless overwork meant she had no time to process the original triggers, so unprocessed bicycle and footstep cues continued to flash unbidden, and the strategies only deepened her belief that her body was the enemy. The emotional weight of the memory directly fueled her negative appraisals, convincing her she would snap if left alone, while her belief that she was fundamentally unsafe made the memories feel more urgent and unmanageable. Now, at nineteen, Kiana sits on the dock behind her rental house, staring at the water she once navigated without fear. The trauma account still explains why her particular triggers are so potent: the event was not just loud, but deeply personal, a sudden rupture where her hesitation was witnessed by her own conscience. She came to seek help because the memory of the event, though imageless, still floods her with guilt whenever a bicycle passes the slipway. She hopes therapy might finally untangle the belief that her body is the enemy, but she is most afraid that if she stops working or stops watching screens, the full weight of her failure to protect will crush her. For now, she watches the footsteps of passing fishermen and braces for a body that reacts before her mind can catch up, waiting for a way to step off the trawler and finally rest.
